prompt.context: A large food conglomerate (such as a Nabisco or Kraft) has a small plant in Maine that produces apple juice from one specific type of apple which is grown locally. The apple juice is premium priced and positioned. The company bought the plant from a local farmer cooperative a few years back with the hopes that the company could increase the plant's capacity through better management. The plant is currently operating at full capacity. There was an accident at the plant recently where a worker broke his leg. This incident prompted a review by OSHA (the government review agency in charge of occupational safety). OSHA has informed the company that an additional $2 million investment is needed to bring the plant up to current safety standards.
prompt.question: You have been hired by the company to help it decide what it should do. Specifically, you need to provide your client with a list of options and then identify the one that you recommend.

clarifying_info.a: The apple juice product is breaking even for the company.
There are several other premium apple juice brands. The competition is stiff.

clarifying_info.q: Can supply of the raw material be increased?
clarifying_info.a: There is a raw material constraint — there is a limited number of this specific kind of apple grown each year. You cannot grow more apples or stretch more out of the current supply.

clarifying_info.q: Is there demand for the product?
clarifying_info.a: The demand for the apple juice is strong. Consumer demand is only limited by the availability of supply. The strength of the demand stems from the uniqueness of the product (that special kind of apple).

clarifying_info.q: Can the plant produce a juice concentrate to extend the supply?
clarifying_info.a: Producing a concentrate will not work for this plant — it is too costly to convert machinery and this specific kind of apple does not lend well to such a use.

clarifying_info.q: What are the company's core competencies?
clarifying_info.a: The company's competitive advantage is its marketing expertise and distribution system.

framework: Enumerate all strategic options (get out/sell, status quo/minimum investment, full investment, partnership)
Identify all relevant stakeholders: farmers, customers, company, local community, government regulators, competitors
Assess advantages and disadvantages of each option for each stakeholder
Evaluate internal rate of return / opportunity cost of the $2M investment versus uses elsewhere in the organization
Consider public relations implications of each option (layoffs, safety record, brand perception)
Weigh the resource constraint (fixed apple supply) and breakeven economics against strategic fit with company's core competencies (marketing and distribution, not plant operations)
Arrive at a recommendation and articulate why it best serves the client

questions.prompt: What are all the options available to the client?
questions.guidance: A strong answer enumerates at least three distinct options: (1) exit — shut down or sell the plant; (2) status quo / minimum investment — invest only the $2M required by OSHA to maintain current operations; (3) full investment — invest above the minimum in both facility and human resources to grow the plant; (4) partnership — transfer plant operations to the original farmer cooperative while the company retains marketing and distribution rights. Being thorough and listing all options before narrowing is explicitly valued here.

questions.prompt: Given the information available, which option do you recommend and why?
questions.guidance: The recommended option is to arrange a partnership agreement with the local farmer cooperative that originally sold the plant. Key reasoning: (a) the product is only breaking even, so a $2M mandatory investment has a weak return; (b) there is a hard raw-material ceiling on upside — more investment cannot grow revenue; (c) the company's core competency is marketing and distribution, not plant operations; (d) a partnership lets the company retain the premium brand and distribution relationship while offloading operational and safety risk. A pure shutdown/sale is second-best — it avoids the investment but sacrifices brand presence and has adverse PR implications (layoffs, publicizing the safety incident). Simply investing the minimum is the weakest option because it perpetuates a breakeven business with no path to improved returns.

questions.prompt: What are the public relations and stakeholder risks of the exit/sell option?
questions.guidance: Layoffs in the local Maine community; negative press coverage linking the company to the safety accident; risk that news leaks that safety standards were substandard before the OSHA review; potential damage to the premium brand image. These risks favor a partnership structure over an outright shutdown or sale.

brainstorming.prompt: Who are the stakeholders affected by this decision, and what are their interests?

categories.name: Company (client)
ideas: Avoid a cash-negative $2M investment in a breakeven business
Leverage core competency in marketing and distribution
Minimize legal and reputational liability from the safety incident

categories.name: Local farmers / cooperative
ideas: Secure a stable market and distribution channel for their unique apple crop

categories.name: Employees
ideas: Job security and safe working conditions
Continuity of employment regardless of ownership structure

categories.name: Customers
ideas: Continued access to a unique premium product
Confidence that the brand maintains quality and safety standards

categories.name: Competitors
ideas: Monitor whether the brand exits the premium segment, creating an opening
Potential acquisition of the plant or brand if sold

recommendation: Recommend a partnership agreement with the original farmer cooperative: transfer plant operations to the cooperative while the company retains exclusive marketing and distribution rights for the premium apple juice brand

This structure allows the company to exit capital-intensive, breakeven plant operations while preserving the brand, the unique apple-supply relationship, and the distribution channel — all aligned with the company's core competencies
risks: Partnership negotiations may be complex or fail; the cooperative may lack capital to assume plant operations and fund the OSHA-required $2M upgrade
Loss of direct operational control could create quality-consistency risks for a premium-positioned product
If the partnership collapses, the company may face a harder exit with worse terms
next_steps: Initiate discussions with the farmer cooperative to gauge interest and negotiate terms
Conduct financial due diligence on the cooperative's ability to fund the $2M OSHA upgrade
Define contractual quality and supply guarantees to protect the premium brand
Develop a PR and employee communications plan to manage the transition
